query: For transition-metal catalysts, formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis explaining what governs catalytic activity, selectivity, or durability and why. Specify an unnamed controlled comparison that would reveal the governing cause, the observations predicted relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, supporting prior evidence, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Incorporating Cu into a Pt catalyst to form a Pt/Cu single‐atom alloy weakens the adsorption strength of disruptive intermediates (e.g., propylene) and thereby slows down deactivation by carbon deposition.
generation.material_initial_state: Transition‐metal catalysts composed of pure Pt nanoparticles that bind intermediates strongly.
generation.intervention: Deliberate formation of a Pt/Cu single‐atom alloy via controlled composition change.
generation.conditions: Under reaction conditions (e.g., propylene activation) where strong adsorbate binding leads to catalyst poisoning, at moderate temperatures and similar gas compositions for both catalysts.
generation.structural_mediator: Modification of the local electronic structure at Pt sites by isolated Cu atoms.
generation.mechanism: The isolated Cu atoms in the alloy modulate the Pt d‐band structure, decreasing the binding energy of adsorbed reactive intermediates. This weaker interaction minimizes the formation of deactivating carbon deposits and improves catalyst durability.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to pure Pt nanoparticle catalysts, the Pt/Cu SAA catalyst will exhibit a lower temperature desorption peak (measured by TPD), reduced carbon buildup, and slower activity decay over time.
generation.baseline: Catalytic performance and deactivation behavior of pure Pt nanoparticle catalysts under identical reaction conditions.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold for transition‐metal catalysts experiencing poisoning due to strong adsorbate binding (e.g., in propylene deactivation scenarios); deviations may occur under conditions with significantly different reactant environments or extreme temperatures.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative improvements in binding energy and durability may vary with reaction specifics, catalyst preparation methods, and particle size effects. Further experiments are necessary to define the optimal composition and conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two catalysts: one with pure Pt nanoparticles and another with a Pt/Cu single‐atom alloy. Expose both catalysts to propylene reaction conditions known to induce poisoning. Use temperature-programmed desorption (TPD) to compare adsorbate binding energies, monitor catalytic activity over time, and quantify carbon deposition on the catalyst surfaces.
measurements: TPD peak temperatures for propylene adsorption
Catalytic activity decay rates over continuous operation
Carbon deposition levels (via surface analysis techniques)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Pt/Cu SAA catalyst does not exhibit a significantly lower TPD desorption temperature, slower decline in catalytic activity, and reduced carbon deposition compared to the pure Pt nanoparticle catalyst, then the hypothesis would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The development of new catalysts with simultaneously enhanced activity and selectivity is always the ultimate goal of researchers. In heterogeneous catalysis, the screening of new catalyst can be simply guided by the Sabatier principle. It indicates that the best catalysts should bind reactive intermediates with suitable interaction strength: neither too strong that leads to surface poisoning, nor too weak which fails to activate the reactants. The principle behind this phenomenon can be attributed to the existence of scaling properties of adsorption energies on transition metal surfaces, and various linear scaling relationships have been developed which connect the reaction energy/barriers with binding energy of representative surface species, i.e., descriptors. Therefore, the complicated reaction kinetics can be described by only a few descriptors, which enables fast screening of potential catalytic materials with the help of density functional theory (DFT) calculations.

The temperature-programmed desorption (TPD) of propylene (Supplementary Figure 22) indicates that the interaction between the propylene and metal sites is weaker for Cu nanoparticles and Pt/Cu SAA than that for Pt nanoparticles. This weak interaction minimizes carbon deposits on the active Pt sites to help remain the activity during reaction.

reading.lever: Implement Pt/Cu SAA formation to deliberately lower adsorbate binding strength and mitigate poisoning.
reading.why: This approach, demonstrated for propylene deactivation mitigation, can be extended to probe transition‐metal catalyst activity and durability under controlled comparisons.
